In the fertile fields and boundless prairies, and it was not there. In her rich mines and her vast world commerce, and it was not there. Not until I went into the churches of America and heard her pulpits, aflame with righteousness, did I understand the secret of her genius and power. America is great because she is good, and if America ever ceases to be good, America will cease to be great

meta.description: Not Tocqueville. It is nowhere in Democracy in America, and the earliest printings we could read are American newspapers of 1923 and 1925, longer than the version in circulation today. An 1886 sermon carries an older, different version.

meta.ogDescription: A famous line about American goodness that Tocqueville never wrote. We traced it to American pulpit rhetoric printed in 1923, and to a different 1886 sermon before that.

answer.label: Not Tocqueville — American pulpit rhetoric
answer.authorDates: Unattributed · in print by 1923; a different version by 1886
answer.sourceLine: Tocqueville did not write this, and Wikiquote files it under Misattributed the entry ↗. The negative check is easy to repeat: in the searchable text of both volumes of Democracy in America in the standard Reeve translation, the word commodious occurs exactly once — in a passage about promotion in the army — and the word pulpit does not occur at all volume one ↗. The passage is American, not French. The earliest printing we were able to fetch and read is the Casper Daily Tribune of 15 April 1923, where the search runs through five ‘I sought’ clauses rather than the three of the modern version the 1923 page ↗.

source.heading: The source — and what is actually there
source.excerpt: I went at your bidding, and passed along their thoroughfares of trade. I ascended their mountains and went down their valleys. I visited their manufactories, their commercial markets, and emporiums of trade. I entered their judicial courts and legislative halls. But I sought everywhere in vain for the secret of their success, until I entered the church. It was there, as I listened to the soul-equalizing and soul-elevating principles of the Gospel of Christ, as they fell from Sabbath to Sabbath upon the masses of the people, that I learned why America was great and free, and why France was a slave.
trail: The specialists have ruled on it. Wikiquote lists the passage in its Misattributed section, notes that it is often credited to Democracy in America ‘but erroneously’, and records an appearance in the Herald and Presbyter of 6 September 1922 the Wikiquote entry ↗. We follow that finding and do not claim an origin earlier or more specific than it documents.

It is not in the book. Searching the full text of the Reeve translation of Democracy in America turns up ‘commodious’ a single time, describing the slow but commodious advancement of a peace establishment in an army, and no instance at all of ‘pulpit’ or of any sentence about America ceasing to be good volume one ↗ volume two ↗.

1923, in a Wyoming newspaper. The Casper Daily Tribune of 15 April 1923 prints the passage inside a sermon-like column, introduced as ‘In 1831 a French nobleman came to this country to learn if possible the secret of our success as a nation’ and delivered, supposedly, as he laid the book in his publisher’s hands. It searches five times before it finds an answer: the modern version has dropped the clauses about America’s public school system and about ‘her democratic congress and her matchless constitution’ the 1923 page ↗.

1925, and the credit hardens. The Osceola Times of Arkansas runs the same longer five-search text on 13 February 1925 under the heading ‘The Greatness of America’, now signed off in print as by ‘Alexix de Tocqueville’ — misspelt — ‘in Democracy in America’. Two years earlier the paper had only described a French visitor; by 1925 the fabricated citation is attached the 1925 page ↗.
source.cutTag: Madison C. Peters, Empty Pews, 1886, p. 35
source.excerptNote: This is not the quote. It is its ancestor, printed in a Philadelphia sermon in 1886 and there credited to ‘De Tochneville, the distinguished French statesman’ — a garbled name, and a report supposedly made to the French Senate. Notice what is missing: the sentence everybody remembers, about America being great because she is good, is not in it. The famous ending is a later addition to a passage that was already circulating without it.
source.rightsNote: We assert no copyright status for this wording, because nobody can say who wrote it. What can be said is narrower and useful: the American printings we located and read — the 1923 Casper Daily Tribune, the 1925 Osceola Times, and the 1886 Peters sermon that carries the older version — were all published in the United States well before 1931 and are therefore in the public domain as printings the 1886 sermon ↗. That covers those specific texts, not the shortened modern paraphrase, whose origin is unknown. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Alexis de Tocqueville
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on Tocqueville
author.metaLine: 1805–1859 · French diplomat, political philosopher and historian
author.bio: Alexis de Tocqueville came to the United States in 1831 on a commission from the July Monarchy to examine American prisons and penitentiaries, travelling with his friend Gustave de Beaumont; he was back in France within nine months and published On the Penitentiary System in the United States in 1833. The famous book, Democracy in America, followed in 1835 and 1840 and made him the permanent foreign authority on the American character. That is exactly what makes him useful to a forger: he is a sympathetic outsider whose verdict on America carries weight precisely because he was not American. The 1923 newspaper version gives the game away by saying he came ‘to learn if possible the secret of our success as a nation’. He came to look at prisons.

cite.sourceLabel: No source in Tocqueville; earliest printing located

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: This is a fabrication with an unusually well-documented career: you can watch it acquire its famous last sentence, lose two of its clauses, and pick up a fake page-citation, all in American print.

items.why: Nothing like it is in Democracy in America. Wikiquote records the attribution as erroneous the entry ↗, and the searchable Reeve translation contains neither the vocabulary nor the sentiment volume two ↗.

items.scope: What the older version looked like
items.why: Madison Clinton Peters, preaching on the Sunday question, quotes ‘De Tochneville’ reporting to the French Senate that he sought the secret of American success in vain until he entered the church. The wording shares almost nothing with the modern text except its shape, and the celebrated closing sentence is absent page 35 ↗.

The 1923 and 1925 printings both search for America’s greatness in her public school system and her institutions of learning, and in her democratic congress and her matchless constitution. Both clauses have since been dropped. ‘Boundless forests’ became ‘boundless prairies’, ‘pulpits flame with righteousness’ became ‘pulpits, aflame with righteousness’, and ‘America is great because America is good’ became ‘because she is good’ the 1923 text ↗.

items.who: The reference to Democracy in America
items.why: In 1923 the passage is introduced only as the remark of an unnamed French nobleman. By February 1925 an Arkansas weekly is printing it over the signature ‘Alexix de Tocqueville in Democracy in America’ — a citation to a book that does not contain it the 1925 page ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: Nobody knows who wrote it. It is American pulpit rhetoric that was already in newspapers by 1923, descended from an older and different passage printed in 1886, and it was never in any book of Tocqueville’s Wikiquote, Misattributed ↗.

context.heading: Why it survives
lead: It has been quoted from the White House down, and it survives because it is doing a job no real Tocqueville sentence can do. He wrote long, cool, qualified analysis; this is a benediction. It gives an American audience a flattering verdict and puts it in the mouth of the one foreign observer everyone has heard of.

The tell is structural. Real Tocqueville argues; this recites. A run of parallel search clauses closing on a chiasmus is the architecture of a sermon peroration, not of a chapter in a work of political sociology — and, sure enough, the oldest version we can find is a sermon.
detailsBody: 1831: Tocqueville arrives in the United States on a commission to inspect prisons, not to find the secret of American greatness.
1835, 1840: Democracy in America is published in two volumes. The passage is in neither.
1886: Madison C. Peters prints an older, different version in a Philadelphia sermon collection, crediting ‘De Tochneville’. The famous last sentence is not yet there.
1922: Wikiquote records an appearance in the Herald and Presbyter of 6 September — a Presbyterian weekly, which fits the passage’s pulpit origins.
15 April 1923: the Casper Daily Tribune prints the longer five-search version, attributed to an unnamed French nobleman.
13 February 1925: the Osceola Times prints the same text signed ‘Alexix de Tocqueville in Democracy in America’. The fake citation is now attached.
Later twentieth century: two of the search clauses fall away and the shorter version in circulation today takes shape.
context.pull: In 1923 it was a French nobleman’s remark. By 1925 it had a book and a page behind it. Neither was true.
